one_liner: Rust typesetting system (markup language, compiler, CLI) that built mail-merge PDFs 3-5x faster than pdfLaTeX in one shootout.
what_it_does: Compiles .typ markup (with an embedded scripting language, set/show rules, math and bibliographies) to PDF, PNG, SVG or HTML via the single-binary CLI (typst compile, typst watch) or the typst Rust crate, where the host implements the World trait to supply sources, files and fonts. It replaces a LaTeX toolchain rather than plugging into one: there is no TeX compatibility, documents and templates must be rewritten in Typst syntax, and it can load data files itself (the benchmark template calls xml() on the input), which is why the benchmarked mail merge needs no external templating step.
how_it_is_fast: Incremental compilation through comemo, constrained memoization: layout and evaluation functions are #[comemo::memoize]d over Tracked inputs that record which parts of the World or introspector a call actually read, so a cached result is reused whenever those parts are unchanged, across edits in watch mode and across identical content within one run. Since 0.12 the layout engine splits the document at explicit page breaks into page runs and lays them out in parallel (engine.parallelize over Item::Run in typst-layout pages/mod.rs; changelog: 'typical speedups are 2-3x for larger documents'). Justified paragraphs use Knuth-Plass optimal line breaking with a two-pass scheme: a cheap pass with approximate metrics yields an upper bound on cost that prunes the exact pass (linebreak_optimized_approximate then linebreak_optimized_bounded). Hyphenation comes from hypher's embedded automata, and the CLI is one native binary with no format files to load: the whole one-page benchmark compile took 105.7 ms.
when_to_use: Batch generation of many similar documents from structured data (letters, invoices, contract notes) where templates can be written in Typst: the speedata shootout and Zerodha's contract-note pipeline (search snippet) both report several-fold speedups over LaTeX.
Interactive or watch-mode editing of long documents, where memoized relayout recompiles only what changed.
Multi-page output on multi-core machines: page runs separated by explicit page breaks are laid out in parallel (tune with --jobs).
Containers and CI where a single static binary is simpler than a TeX Live installation.
when_not_to_use: Existing LaTeX documents, classes or journal templates: there is no TeX compatibility, so every template must be ported and many CTAN packages have no Typst equivalent.

When you need a stable performance profile across upgrades: open regressions include #7102 (10,000 identical list items: about 200 ms on 0.13, 1.5 s on 0.14-rc1) and #8611 (a 300-page document with a glossary: 1 min 17 s and 32 GB on 0.14.2, 14 min and 41 GB on 0.15.0), and, per the verifier's notes, texlode/luatex-benchmark measured 0.14+ incremental edits 1.6-2.2x slower than 0.12/0.13 on x86.

Table-heavy or introspection-heavy documents without testing first: #4560 (slow PDF compilation with many tables) is open, and memory can grow very large (#8611 reports 32-41 GB; #3150 and #8628 request limits and graceful out-of-memory handling).
Hosts with very many installed fonts: the CLI scans every system font file at start-up (#8561 reports about 50 s on one Linux machine); use --ignore-system-fonts with --font-path.
C or C++ embedding: there is no C API; drive the CLI as a subprocess or write a Rust wrapper.

integration.form: CLI binary (typst-cli) or Rust crate (typst plus typst-layout, typst-pdf and related workspace crates)
integration.dependencies: Pure Rust; notable crates include comemo, rayon, hypher, rustybuzz, ttf-parser, fontdb, icu_segmenter/icu_properties, wasmi for plugins and krilla (pinned git revision) for PDF export
integration.platforms: Any platform Rust targets; the speedata numbers are from macOS on Apple M4
integration.thread_safety: Compiler is internally multithreaded (layout, plugins); since 0.12 World implementations must be Send + Sync.

gotchas: Parallel layout only kicks in at explicit page breaks (pagebreak() or separate page runs); a single long flowing document gets less benefit.
Performance is version-sensitive (see the open regression issues), so pin the version you benchmarked; 0.14.0 and 0.14.1 also shipped a wasmi use-after-free fixed in 0.14.2.
Hyphenation uses hypher, which ignores the TeX \hyphenation{} exception lists, so line breaks can differ from LaTeX on exception words.
Tagged (accessible) PDF output arrived in 0.14; the --no-pdf-tags opt-out is hidden and marked deprecated in the current CLI source (removal planned for the 0.17 cycle).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It is the only full typesetting system in this category: pick it when you need finished paged PDFs from markup or data, and pick Parley (rich-text layout) or hypher (hyphenation only, which Typst itself uses) when you are building your own layout or rendering stack.
verified_claims_summary: speedata's hyperfine runs on a MacBook Air M4 (Typst 0.14.2 against pdfTeX 1.40.24 and LuaHBTeX 1.15.0 from TeX Live 2022) put Typst at 105.7 ms for a one-page letter (3.1x faster than pdflatex, 4.9x than LuaLaTeX, derived from page data) and 156.6 ms for 500 identical letters (4.55x and 15.0x), with the LaTeX times including a Python and Jinja2 templating step. Typst's 500-page run used several cores (pagebreak() between letters enables parallel page-run layout) while pdflatex is single-threaded: on total CPU time (user plus system) the 500-page gap is 308 ms against 716 ms, about 2.3x, and the marginal cost per extra page is about 1.9x lower (both derived from page data), so roughly half of the 4.55x wall-clock win comes from parallelism and lower start-up. Zerodha's production report (blog blocked, search snippet only) gives about 3-4x faster than LaTeX overall and about 1 min against about 18 min with lualatex for 2000+ page table documents.
status_note: Very active (0.15.1 released 2026-07-17, commits through 2026-09-30, 2.9M crates.io downloads, Apache-2.0); copyable as a Rust crate or used as a CLI, not as a C/C++ library.
